extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature/classical drama; dramatists and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing and judging poetry and tragedy according to Aristotelian Poetics (plot, character, style, music, and staging). Intended to guide analysts, editors, and dramatic writers working in classical or theory-informed traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative art simulates (mimics) action; 'creative art simulates with things differing in kind just as reproductive art simulates with Colour, Figure and Sound.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the object of imitation (action) from mere reproduction of sensory features; use imitation to represent actions that can be apprehended as complete events. See contrast with reproductive arts which imitate qualities such as colour or sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is 'mimesis of an action that is serious (σπουδαῖα), complete (τελεία), and of a certain magnitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must present a whole action (not a series of loosely connected episodes), be serious in subject-matter, and have sufficient magnitude/length to accomplish its artistic ends (unity and emotional effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action / Plot Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic action must have 'a beginning, middle and end' and 'unity of theme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must form a cohesive whole in which events follow by necessity or probability from one another; avoid episodic or miscellaneous assemblages of scenes. The beginning introduces the action without itself depending on prior events; the middle follows by necessity; the end follows from what precedes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Structure: Complex vs Simple; Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots involve 'reversal' (peripeteia) and 'disclosure'/'recognition' (anagnorisis), whereas simple plots lack these features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer complex plots that produce stronger artistic effects via reversal and recognition; these devices should arise naturally from the plot's internal logic rather than by accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity in Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Events should follow 'by law'—that is by necessity or probability—so that the mind accepts the sequence; the audience infers causes from consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that the subsequent events are credible consequences of preceding ones; avoid arbitrary incidents that break the causal or probable chain of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (Length and Scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must be 'of a certain magnitude'—sufficient size to portray the whole action properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the play is long enough to present the full sequence (beginning, middle, end) and to generate the intended emotional impact; avoid undue compression that sacrifices necessary development or undue expansion that dilutes unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Appropriateness and Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be 'appropriate' (fitting the action) and 'consistent'—their actions must accord with their established character and with what is credible for such persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters whose choices and dispositions follow from their natures and circumstances; avoid inconsistent behaviour or unexplained transformations that undermine plot credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Status of Characters (Relative Virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are 'either relatively virtuous or vicious' (balanced alternatives relative to a standard), not necessarily wholly good or wholly bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer protagonists of a certain quality or standing (often better or noble) but with a mix of qualities; use relative valuations (better/worse) rather than absolute polarities to make characters psychologically plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Deus Ex Machina / Unmotivated Introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle criticizes solutions by arbitrary or external intervention (deus ex machina) and the sudden, unprepared appearance of characters (example: objections about Aegeus in Medea versus the chariot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve the plot by introducing an agent or device that has no antecedent in the action's causal chain; all decisive appearances or solutions must be prepared for by prior elements in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Detail to Induce Belief (Romancing Technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: When inventing (romancing), include particulars that the mind will take as signs of truth—'add that other thing; for the mind, knowing that law to be true, falsely supposes that the first is real.' (Bath‑scene example from Homer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make fictional incidents believable, supply concrete, law‑like details that invite the audience to infer the existence of unseen elements; plentiful, specific detail increases plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esoteric Style: Brevity, Technicality, Interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: An esoteric style uses extreme brevity, artificial vocabulary/syntax, high technicality and cross‑dependence of passages so that the text assumes knowledge of other parts or glosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that esotericism renders a work inaccessible to general readers and often requires oral instruction; use this style only when addressing an initiated audience or for pedagogical/disciplinary purposes. The Poetics itself evidences such interdependence with other Aristotelian works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and Referential Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many passages presuppose knowledge of other works (e.g., references to Categories, Ethics, Topics, Metaphysics); the Poetics relies on cross‑references for full intelligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing theoretical or densely allusive material, provide glosses or make referents explicit for less initiated readers; otherwise accept that comprehension will depend on familiarity with the wider system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus: Integral but Secondary Role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus has an artistic function and should be part of the whole action, but it is subordinate to the action (Aristotle comments on the chorus's place and faults in Euripides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus to enhance the dramatic action (mood, commentary, ritual function), but ensure it does not usurp the plot's primary functions; choral passages should be appropriate to the progression of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) as Least Artistic Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (stagecraft, visual effect) is less a matter of poetical art and more of machinery and stage resources; it is the least artistic element compared to plot and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on plot, character and thought to achieve the central tragic effects rather than spectacular devices; use spectacle to support, not substitute for, intrinsic dramatic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Language (Style and Ordinary Language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author discusses 'usage of ordinary language' and cautions about technical or forced expressions; Homer’s prosaic details are defended as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction that suits the subject, audience and mode—ordinary language may solve certain difficulties and enhance clarity; avoid unnecessary ornamentation and commonplaces that weaken poetic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and Harmony / Love of Order as Origin of Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from Mimicry plus Harmony and Rhythm; these belong to the category 'order' and are 'according to nature'—infants delight in them and operations are aided by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate measured rhythm and harmonic organization as fundamental to poetic effect; structure and order are natural principles that underpin audience pleasure and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and Intellectual Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poetics presupposes philosophical concepts (e.g., energeia, praxis teleia) so that the identification of tragedy's theme with 'happiness' follows from prior theoretical premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the ideas and themes dramatized cohere with the conceptual framework you assume; readers acquainted with the theoretical background will apprehend deeper identifications—if not, provide exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Commonplace and Tasteless Ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle criticizes commonplace lines and tasteless ornaments (e.g., some tragic lines called 'commonplace'); trivial or over‑familiar phrases weaken poetic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for fresh, apt expression rather than hackneyed phrases; ornamental language must serve the action and character rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Functionality and Social Role
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should have functions related to the whole (social rank, capacity for virtue dependent on role—ruler vs humbler members), and certain virtues/capacities are constrained by social position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters whose capabilities and moral possibilities accord with their social role and the play's internal logic; recognize that audience expectations about capacity affect believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing Generality by Consequences (Use of 'Consequences' to Detect Charlatanry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amateur can detect charlatanry by 'the consequences,' i.e., signs that follow from a claimed science or craft even if the amateur does not know the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition and criticism, use observable consequences and concrete signs to evaluate plausibility and artistic truth; ensure that actions produce credible side‑effects the audience can recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and Economy of Narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle notes comparative compression (e.g., Oedipus) versus expansive epic forms; a tragic plot may need to be more compressed than epic to preserve unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ narrative economy so that only what serves the central action remains; compress where necessary to maintain intensity and unity, expand only when it deepens causal understanding.
